How to Build a Dedicated Remote BIM Team

A remote BIM team works when it has a lead, your standards and a rhythm of reporting. How to set one up.

A dedicated remote BIM team is a group of modelers and coordinators who work only on your project, with a lead who is accountable for their output. Set up well, it gives the capacity of an in-house team without the hiring. Set up badly, it becomes a group of individuals waiting for instructions.

1. Size the team from the scope

Start from deliverables and dates: which disciplines, which LOD, how many levels or zones, and the milestones. Size the team for the next phase, not the whole project, and plan how it scales.

2. Appoint a lead

The single most important role. The lead plans the team’s work, runs internal coordination and QA, and is your one point of contact. Without a lead, your BIM manager ends up managing every individual.

3. Onboard to your standards

Share the BEP, templates, families, naming conventions and a sample of good output. A short onboarding session and a first small task show quickly whether standards are understood.

4. Work in your CDE

The team should work in your CDE with named accounts and permissions that follow your security policy. Avoid emailing models back and forth.

5. Agree hours and rhythm

Set overlap hours for calls, a daily or twice-weekly progress update and a weekly review of output against the programme. Time-zone differences can work in your favour when handovers are planned.

6. Build QA into the routine

Use a checklist from your BEP before every issue, and review a sample of output yourself in the first weeks.

7. Plan continuity

Keep handover notes current and identify backups for key roles so the team survives changes in people.

ENGISOFT builds dedicated BIM teams with their own BIM lead, working remotely, onsite or both.
